messages.subject: Ecometric model with spatial information
messages.body_plain:
I consider to derive area-level variables from a questionnaire using the ecometric approach (Raudenbush SW, Sampson RJ. Ecometrics: Toward a Science of Assessing Ecological Settings, with Application to the Systematic Social Observation of Neighborhoods. doi:10.1111/0081-1750.00059 <https://doi.org/10.1111/0081-1750.00059>).

This method involves fitting a multilevel model where individual responses to the questionnaire are nested within individuals, and these individuals are further nested within larger geographical areas, such as neighborhoods.

The ecometric approach enables the assessment of area-level characteristics by accounting for both individual and contextual factors. The area-level deviation serves as an indicator of the construct being measured by the questionnaire (e.g., community cohesion or neighborhood safety) for the respective areas.

Considering the ordinal nature of the items in question, and the fact that it is probably beneficial to incorporate spatial information ( Verbitsky Savitz N, Raudenbush SW. Exploiting Spatial Dependence to Improve Measurement of Neighborhood Social Processes. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9531.2009.01221.x <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2009.01221.x>), I think INLA might be a good tool to fit such models.  I believe INLA would be less computationally intense than some STAN-based solution, and I am in any case not aware of many other accessible ways to fit multilevel models with spatial structures.

Unfortunately, I have no experience at all with this... So I would very much appreciate some input on the following:

I consider running the code below, and then extract the random effects of the areas as indicator of the construct for the area.

- Could this be a reasonable approach?.

I am quite sure that the models below would need tweaking or improvements. I am also unsure on how to handle the two random effects components produced when using a BYM2 model for the spatial structure. I suppose both are relevant for the ecometric purpose.

- How could the random effects be appropriately used as ecometric indicators?

# Fit the model
inlafit_survey_ecometric <- inla(response ~ item + f(RandomID) + f(area, model = "bym2", graph = G_area), data = long_survey, family = "pom", control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE), control.predictor = list(link = 1))

summary(inlafit_survey_ecometric)

# Extract the random effects components for the area
re_sp_inlafit_survey_ecometric <- inlafit_survey_ecometric$summary.random$area[1:length(G_area$cc$id), c("ID", "mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")]
re_other_inlafit_survey_ecometric <- inlafit_survey_ecometric$summary.random$area[length(G_area$cc$id)+1:2*length(G_area$cc$id), c("ID", "mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")]

parameter values, including the linear predictor. (see parameter 'a', hence 'a'

If I understand you want to share the random intercept from the biomarker in the survival model for a terminal event? Or you still want to have a random effect in the survival model that is shared in the biomarker model?

In case you want to share the random intercept in the survival model, this can be done directly with INLAjoint, I just added the option to compute the correlation matrix of fixed effects, so you'll have to update INLAjoint to the latest GitHub version:

devtools::install_github('DenisRustand/INLAjoint', build_vignettes = TRUE)

Then the attached code shows how to get the correlation matrix.

On the other hand, if you want to have a frailty term in the survival model shared in the biomarker model (as before), you'll need to keep the (1|id) in the survival formula and the formula update should be the same as in the first code.

Best,
Denis

messages.body_plain:
it seems all doable yes.

if you have country, region, school, class hierarchy, then it would be

 ~ f(region) + f(school) + f(class)

there model="iid" is the default,

you may want some better priors than the default, and you may want to impose
some sum-to-zero constraint to avoid confounding in the mean (and then inflating
the variance)

there are no assumptions that this need to be 'balanced'.

if you want dependence, like spatial, then

f(region) could be  f(region, model="bym2", ...)

etc, same with the others

best way is to make simulated data to make sure its all correct

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The basic use of replicate in inlabru works the same way as for non-SPDE models. The odd one out is actually the inla() SPDE models, where one needs to construct the A matrix first, which is why the w.repl construction is needed there. In inlabru, you would instead supply the replicate information directly in the component definition, e.g. like

+ field(geometry, model=spde, replicate=time)

(Assuming that replications across “time” are desired; replace it with your own variable of choice…)

One can also optionally use a custom mapper for the replicates, which for example would allow interpolation between replicates (this can make sense in some models, but usually it does not; it is more commonly useful for some “group” models).

Finn

Hi,

personally, when I'm not specifically speaking about the
implementation details, I would simply write the continuous
formulation of the model, i.e.

\log \lambda(s) = \eta(s),
{y_i} ~ Poisson process with intensity \lambda(s) on s\in\Omega

where \eta(s) is the linear predictor evaluated at some location s,
and mention that the integral \int \lambda(s) ds in the likelihood is
(with default settings) implemented using a trapezoidal integration
scheme based on the triangulation mesh used to define the spde model.
But if I really needed to write the approximation explicitly, I'd write that

\int_\Omega \lambda(s) ds \approx \sum_{j=1}^J w_j \exp(\eta(s_j)),
where \{(s_j,w_j),j=1,...,J\} is the aforementioned triangular
trapezoidal integration scheme.

This is a basic numerical integration scheme for a sufficiently smooth function.

This is discussed in more generality in the old "Going off grid" paper
and should suffice as reference. (Note: there is a common
misconception about what that paper actually says; ignore the "dual
mesh" stuff; it's only there to illustrate a coincidence in
interpretation of the weights for the default integration scheme; the
weights happen to be equal to _both_ the integral of each basis
function, _and_ the area of each node-connected "dual mesh" cell, but
the dual mesh is not used in any other way. Specifically, it is _not_
used to make aggregated counts; that's a separate choice some people
sometimes make for the \sum_i \log(\lambda(y_i)) part of the
likelihood.)
At the time of writing the Going off grid paper, we weren't yet fully
aware of the difficulty with _non_-trapezoidal integration schemes; if
we had, we should have been more forecul about specific integration
scheme recommendations.

With the addition of the fmesher fm_subdiv() method, it's now easier
to use finer resolution integration scheme that still generate
properly bounded likelihood approximations, for cases where the
default integration scheme isn't sufficient (e.g. when covariates are
at higher resolution than the spde model; we're currently writing
papers about that).

Finn

  (1:contents$length[which(contents$tag=="rr")])

    pred$soil_pH_cat <- as.factor(pred$soil_pH_cat)

  xHyper[,i] <- ps[[i]]$hyperpar
}
xSpace <- xLatent[idSpace,]

xX <- xLatent[idX,]

#Prediction

for (i in 1:nsamp) {
  ID.precision <- xHyper[3,i] #the 3rd row contains precision for rr; same as ps[[i]]$hyperpar[3]

  sample.IIDpred[, i] <- rnorm(nrow(pred), sd = ID.sigma)
}

x1 = pred$lst_day

linpred <-
  as.matrix(Ap %*% xSpace + as.matrix(
    cbind(
      1,
      x1,
      x2
    )
  ) %*% xX + sample.IIDpred)

inv.linpred <- gtools::inv.logit(linpred)

```

  f(s, model = spde) +
  f(rr, model = 'iid', hyper = hyper.prec)

  formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = numtrials,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
  control.family = control.family(link = 'logit'),
  control.predictor = list(
    compute = TRUE,
    link = 1,

Hi,
The inla.spde.result() function can be used to convert to range and variance for inla.spde2.matern models. You can also use inla.tmarginal and related functions directly (e.g. to transform to standard deviation)

The prior is part of the model, so priors for one parameter will affect the estimation of other parameters.

When inla.spde2.matern, you should really specify the parameters for the priors. We discuss how to do that in the 2015 https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19 paper.
Using the default values is not recommended.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you can transform the quantiles like that, yes. The posterior mean and
standard deviation are more involved. However, you can look at the
code to see how the transformation is done.
Also, inla.spde.posterior by default should give you the range and
variance posteriors directly, not just log(range) and log(variance).

The "precision for the lognormal observations" is the precision
parameter of the observation model. See INLA::inla.doc("lognormal")
for the exact definition of the model.

"nugget effect" is just a shorthand name for "random independent
additive noise" when applied to covariance models, and isn't
necessarily a useful term in general, but yes, the observation noise
can be seen as a "nugget effect".
Terminology-wise, I'd say that the "nugget effect" _has_ a variance
(and variance is the inverse of precision), not that it _is_ variance.
But the precision parameter of a _lognormal_ distribution is not the
inverse of the precision of the lognormal variable, unless one uses a
parameterisation that makes that true; it's more common that it's the
precision of the logarithm of the lognormal variable. See the
inla.doc() document for the actual definition in the INLA model
context.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
No, you don’t need kappa; each SPDE model object has its own parameterisation, so the one for spde2.matern is not the same as for spde2.pcmatern.

Usually you can get posterior samples from inla,posterior.sample (or generate()/oredict() when using inlabru) which handles this automatically.
But if you want unconditional samples, you can use inla.spde.precision() followed by inla.qsample(). The first function takes the log of the 2-parameter vector as input,
which is either log(c(range, sigma)) or log(c(sigma, range)) when using the pcmatern model. Try different values to find out the correct order…

Finn

y ~ N(u, sqrt(σ1^2 + σ2^2))
log(u) = a + bx

Do I need to specify anything else to get this working correctly, particularly considering I am modelling the response on the log scale (and I believe that with INLA the model precision/dispersion correspond to the log-transformed response also), but the uncertainties correspond to the identity scale?

Thanks for any help.

messages.subject_clean: Temporally varying coefficient in front of a spatial covariate
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA team,

I would like to incorporate a temporally varying coefficient in my model, in front of a spatial covariate.

A little bit of context: Z is the hourly air temperature on cities (on several consecutive days), imp is the imperviousness and its effect varies along the curse of the day (it is actually indirect, because impervious surfaces store solar energy and release it with a delay). In other words, I'd like to get a varying b coefficient for each hour of the day. I am interested in the marginal posterior of b to see the variable contribution of imperviousness along the day.

Here is a simplified version of my latent process:

Z(s,t) = int + b(hour) * imp(s) + F(s,t)

with
t = hourly timestamps (can be on several consecutive days)
hour = hours of the day from 1 to 24.
F a spde model with AR1 model on group indexed by t

I am struggling to find the best way to implement `b(hour) * imp(s)`, here are some ideas I have, but I am not 100% sure which one is the closest to what I expect:

Option #1: with dynamical model
f(s_imp, model = "spde", group = s_imp.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1" (or "rw1"), cyclic = TRUE))
with s_imp spatiotemporal indexes weighted with imp and temporal with hour.
The problem is I cannot extract separated estimates of b evolving with time, and I am not sure about the use of the weighted spde for this part of my model.

Option #2: seasonal model
Here I have a doubt because it is generally implemented with a time covariate and no interaction with another specific spatial covariate:
f(t, model = "seasonal", season.length = 24)
I would like something like
f(imp, model = "seasonal", season.length = 24, time.index = t)
so that I can have b(1), ...., b(24) marginals.

Option #3: with iid model
f(imp, model = "iid", group = hour, control.group = list(model = ?))
or
f(imp, model = "iid", group = t, control.group = list(model = "seasonal", season.length = 24))
Here I will have independent b(1), ..., b(24), right?

Sorry for the very long message.
Just wanted to add a huge thank you for your amazing work done on this library, and on the "customer service". You deserve the Nobel prize of the best open source geostatistic library.

Eva

messages.body_plain:
This is more of a conceptual question, not a software-related issue.

I have a question regarding the use of the 1D-SPDE with Matérn covariance for a time series problem. My data has two columns: time and y, where time is discrete (1, 2, 3, …), and for now, we can assume y is Gaussian.

I am familiar with AR/ARIMA/RW1/RW2 models, where the model fit references only past values i.e. Y(t) = b0 + b1*Y(t-1).

Does the SPDE approach handle this kind of time-dependence internally? For example, if I fix the range at 10 (so that observations within a distance of 10 have more influence on the current point), and I’m modeling at time t=40, I expect the model to mainly use observations from time 30 to 39 to influence the fit at time 40. However, since time points 41 to 50 are also within the distance of 10, does the SPDE model also use those future observations in the fit?

Do correct my thinking on the range if I got it wrong.

I hope this is clear. Thank you for your help!

For 1D, the SPDE with alpha=1 is the continuous version of AR(1), and alpha=2 is like an AR(2) model. Since you have an observation model on top of this, the posterior distribution isn’t a Markov process anymore, but yes, the discrete time AR and continuous time 1st and 2nd order SPDEs will behave similarly to each other (except that the matern model with alpha=2 leads to a specific subset of AR(2) models).
This of course assumes that the temporal resolution used for the SPDE finite element construction has sufficient resolution (i,e, at most distance 1 between the mesh knots).
Finn
